items.prose: A car park charges £2.40 for each hour or part of an hour. Its ticket machine works this out.
items.question: Is the machine's charging rule a program or a model?

options.text: A program: a person wrote the exact rule
A model: it learned the price from past tickets
options.why: The price is set by the owner and typed in. Nothing is found from examples.

feedback.correct: A person wrote the rule, so it is a program.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask where the rule came from.

explain.text: The owner sets £2.40 an hour, and someone typed that rule in. A model would have found its rule from examples.

items.prose: A card company keeps past payments with: amount, country, hour of day, and fraud or not.
items.question: Which column is the label for a fraud model?

options.why: The amount is seen the moment a payment is made: a feature.
The country is known at once: a feature.
The hour is known at once: a feature.

feedback.correct: Fraud or not is what the model must say.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which column is unknown for a new payment?

explain.text: Amount, country and hour arrive with the payment. Whether it is fraud is the unknown. That is the label.

items.prose: An airline predicts, at booking time, whether a flight will arrive late. Columns: day of week, departure airport, minutes late on arrival.
items.question: Which column is a leak?

options.why: The day is known at booking: a fair feature.
The airport is known at booking: a fair feature.

feedback.correct: Minutes late is only known after landing.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which number arrives after booking?

explain.text: At booking the flight has not flown. Minutes late on arrival nearly is the label and is not known in time. It is a leak.

items.prose: Emails have 1, 2, 4, 6 and 8 links. Those with 2, 6 and 8 links are spam.
items.question: How many does the rule **spam when links are at least 4** get right?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each email against the rule.

byKey.wrong-count: 2 is how many it gets wrong: the emails with 2 and 4 links.
byKey.strict: You treated 4 links as below the threshold. At least 4 includes 4, so that email is called spam and is wrong.

explain.text: The rule calls 4, 6 and 8 spam and 1, 2 not spam. It is wrong on 2 (spam missed) and 4 (false alarm). So 3 of 5 are right.

items.prose: A threshold gets 14 of 16 training emails right.
items.question: What is its accuracy, as a percentage?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the number right by 16.

byKey.count: You typed 14 as a percentage. Divide by 16 first.

explain.text: Accuracy is right over total: $\tfrac{14}{16} = 0.875$, which is 87.5%.

items.prose: Model P scores 100% on its training data and 64% on test data. Model Q scores 88% on training and 85% on test.
items.question: Which should a firm use on new data?

options.why: 100% on training proves little: a memoriser always gets it. P drops to 64% on new data.
Averages mix in training scores. Judge on the test data alone.

feedback.correct: Q: 85% against 64% on data neither model saw.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the test score.

explain.text: A perfect training score is easy to reach by memorising. On test data Q gets 85% and P 64%. Use Q.

items.prose: A memoriser stored emails with 0, 1, 3, 4 and 7 links. New emails arrive with 1, 2, 7 and 8 links.
items.question: How many of the new emails can it answer at all?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which new link counts did it store?

byKey.all: Only link counts it stored can be looked up. It never saw 2 or 8.
byKey.stored: 5 is how many emails it stored. Count the new ones it can look up.

explain.text: A memoriser only looks up what it stored. Of 1, 2, 7 and 8 it stored 1 and 7. So it answers 2 and is silent on the other two.

items.prose: The rule **spam when links are at least 4** meets four kept-back emails. They have 3, 4, 6 and 9 links; the first three are spam and the last is not.
items.question: What is its test score, as a percentage?

feedback.correct: Right on 4 and 6, wrong on 3 and 9: 50%.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply the rule to each of the four, then divide by 4.

byKey.three: 75% would mean 3 right. Check 9 links: the rule says spam, but it is not.
byKey.one: 25% is 1 right. Check 6 links: spam, and the rule says spam.

explain.text: The rule misses the spam with 3 links and flags the email with 9. It is right on 4 and 6, so $\tfrac{2}{4} = 50\%$.

items.prose: A team tries ten thresholds on its 50 test emails. It reports the best score, 96%, as its test score.
items.question: What is wrong with that 96%?

options.text: The test emails chose the threshold, so 96% is not a test score
Nothing: 96% on 50 emails is a fair estimate
options.why: The 50 emails picked the winner from ten. Scoring on them again flatters the model.

options.text: Ten thresholds are too few to try
options.why: Trying more on the same emails would flatter it even more.

options.text: 50 emails is far too many for a test
options.why: 50 is a fine size. The fault is that they were used to choose.

feedback.correct: Choosing on the test set makes it training data.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask whether the test emails helped choose.

explain.text: The test set must play no part in choosing. Here it picked the best of ten thresholds, so 96% is a training score in disguise. A fresh set is needed.

items.prose: A sat-nav shows distances in miles. It converts kilometres by multiplying by 0.6214.
items.question: Should this step be learned from examples?

options.text: No: the exact rule is known, so write it
Yes: models are always more accurate
options.why: A model would only approximate 0.6214. The written rule is exact.
Journeys add nothing: the conversion is a fixed number.

feedback.correct: The exact rule is known, so write it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Is there a perfect rule already?

explain.text: Multiplying by 0.6214 is exact. Learning from examples is for rules nobody can write down. This is not one.
